    <div class="article-header">
        <div class="article-meta">
            <span
                style="background: linear-gradient(135deg, #10b981, #059669); color: white; padding: 0.3rem 0.8rem; border-radius: 4px; font-weight: 600;"><i
                    class="fas fa-sync-alt"></i> UPDATED</span>
            <span><i class="far fa-calendar"></i> Updated: December 18, 2025</span>
            <span><i class="far fa-clock"></i> 14 min read</span>
            <span><i class="fas fa-tag"></i> Ransomware</span>
            <span><i class="fas fa-globe"></i> 17 Countries Affected</span>
        </div>

        <h1 class="article-title">Gentlemen Ransomware: The "Polite" Threat Ripping Through Corporate Networks</h1>
        <p class="article-subtitle">Don't let the name fool you—this Go-based ransomware variant is anything but
            courteous. With BYOVD attacks, GPO manipulation, and a growing victim count across 17 countries, here's
            what you need to know about this sophisticated threat actor.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="hero-image" style="background: none; height: auto;">
        <img src="/images/gentlemen_ransomware.png" alt="Gentlemen Ransomware Threat"
            style="width: 100%; max-width: 1200px; height: auto; border-radius: 12px; box-shadow: 0 10px 30px rgba(255, 76, 76, 0.3);" loading="lazy">
    </div>

    <div class="article-content">

Key Takeaways

  • A new ransomware cartel dubbed 'The Gentlemen' has emerged, utilizing highly polite, corporate-style communication with victims.
  • Despite their polite facade, they are ruthless in their extortion tactics and utilize advanced double-extortion methods.
  • They specifically target mid-market financial and legal firms holding highly sensitive client data.
        <div class="alert-box">
            <strong>🚨 ACTIVE THREAT:</strong> Gentlemen ransomware is actively targeting organizations worldwide as
            of December 2025. If you haven't reviewed your EDR configurations, driver policies, and Active Directory
            security recently, consider this your wake-up call.
        </div>

        <h2>When Ransomware Gets "Sophisticated"</h2>
        <p>I've been tracking ransomware groups for years now, and every once in a while, a new player emerges that
            makes you pause and take notice. The <strong>Gentlemen ransomware gang</strong>—first identified in
            August 2025—is one of those groups that demands attention.</p>

        <p>The irony of the name isn't lost on me. There's nothing gentlemanly about stealing your data, killing
            your security tools, and then demanding ransom while threatening to leak everything publicly. But I
            suppose even cybercriminals appreciate a bit of dark humor. Or maybe it's a psychological play—who
            wouldn't want to negotiate with a "gentleman"?</p>

        <p>What sets this group apart isn't their audacity—it's their <strong>technical sophistication</strong>.
            This isn't a script kiddie operation buying ransomware-as-a-service and hoping for the best. These are
            skilled operators using advanced techniques that would make many red teamers envious. The combination of
            BYOVD attacks, GPO manipulation, and a Go-based payload shows a level of operational maturity that's
            concerning.</p>

        <div class="stats-grid">
            <div class="stat-card">
                <div class="number">17</div>
                <div class="label">Countries Hit</div>
            </div>
            <div class="stat-card">
                <div class="number">BYOVD</div>
                <div class="label">Attack Method</div>
            </div>
            <div class="stat-card">
                <div class="number">Go</div>
                <div class="label">Language</div>
            </div>
            <div class="stat-card">
                <div class="number">2x</div>
                <div class="label">Extortion Model</div>
            </div>
        </div>

        <h2>The Technical Arsenal: A Deep Dive</h2>
        <p>What makes Gentlemen particularly dangerous is their combination of techniques. Each one is effective on
            its own, but together they create a formidable attack chain that's difficult to detect and even harder
            to stop once it's in motion. Let's break down what they're working with:</p>

        <div class="technique-card">
            <h4><i class="fas fa-microchip"></i> BYOVD - Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver</h4>
            <p style="color: var(--text-secondary); margin: 0;">This is the cornerstone of their attack chain. The
                attackers deploy legitimate but vulnerable signed drivers onto victim systems. Because these drivers
                are properly signed by trusted vendors like Gigabyte, MSI, or ASUS, most security tools let them
                through without question.</p>
            <p style="color: var(--text-secondary); margin: 1rem 0 0 0;">Once loaded into the kernel (Ring 0), these
                vulnerable drivers are exploited to terminate EDR agents, antivirus processes, and backup services.
                Your expensive CrowdStrike or SentinelOne deployment? Neutralized before the encryption even starts.
            </p>
        </div>

        <h3>How BYOVD Works: Step by Step</h3>
        <p>Understanding the BYOVD attack chain is crucial for defenders. Here's exactly how Gentlemen executes
            this technique:</p>

        <ol>
            <li><strong>Driver Deployment:</strong> The attackers drop a legitimate but vulnerable signed driver
                (commonly <code>gdrv.sys</code> from Gigabyte or <code>AsIO.sys</code> from ASUS) to the target
                system. Because these drivers are properly signed by trusted hardware vendors, Windows allows them
                to load.</li>
            <li><strong>Kernel-Level Access:</strong> The vulnerable driver contains flaws that allow arbitrary
                read/write to kernel memory. This gives the attacker Ring 0 (kernel) privileges—the highest level of
                access on a Windows system.</li>
            <li><strong>Security Tool Termination:</strong> Using kernel-level access, Gentlemen systematically
                terminates security processes by patching their memory, killing threads, or unloading their drivers.
                Even "tamper-protected" EDR solutions can be defeated at the kernel level.</li>
            <li><strong>Ransomware Deployment:</strong> With security controls disabled, the ransomware payload
                executes without interference, encrypting files and exfiltrating data.</li>
        </ol>

        <div class="code-block">
            # Example vulnerable drivers commonly used in BYOVD attacks:
            gdrv.sys (Gigabyte) - CVE-2018-19320
            AsIO.sys (ASUS) - Arbitrary read/write
            dbutil_2_3.sys (Dell) - CVE-2021-21551
            RTCore64.sys (MSI) - CVE-2019-16098
            WinRing0x64.sys - Multiple hardware vendors
        </div>

        <p><strong>Why is this so effective?</strong> Traditional security tools operate in user mode (Ring 3) while
            these vulnerable drivers operate in kernel mode (Ring 0). It's like trying to fight someone who has the
            high ground—you're at a fundamental disadvantage.</p>

        <div class="technique-card">
            <h4><i class="fas fa-sitemap"></i> GPO Manipulation for Mass Deployment</h4>
            <p style="color: var(--text-secondary); margin: 0;">Instead of manually spreading through the network
                machine by machine (which is slow and increases detection risk), Gentlemen leverages Active
                Directory
                Group Policy Objects to deploy their ransomware at scale.</p>
            <p style="color: var(--text-secondary); margin: 1rem 0 0 0;">Once they compromise a domain controller—or
                even just an account with GPO modification rights—they create or modify a Group Policy that executes
                their payload on every domain-joined machine during the next policy refresh. One click, thousands of
                encrypted endpoints.</p>
        </div>

        <h3>The GPO Attack Chain</h3>
        <p>The abuse of Group Policy is elegant in its simplicity:</p>

        <ol>
            <li><strong>Domain Compromise:</strong> After initial access (often via phishing or VPN credential
                theft), attackers escalate privileges until they have Domain Admin or equivalent rights.</li>
            <li><strong>GPO Creation/Modification:</strong> A new GPO is created or an existing one is modified to
                include a startup script or scheduled task that executes the ransomware binary.</li>
            <li><strong>Staging the Payload:</strong> The ransomware binary is placed in SYSVOL (which replicates to
                all domain controllers) or a network share accessible by all machines.</li>
            <li><strong>Mass Execution:</strong> On the next Group Policy refresh (by default, every 90 minutes for
                computers), every domain-joined machine executes the ransomware. Alternatively, attackers can force
                an immediate refresh using <code>gpupdate /force</code> or invoke-gpupdate via PowerShell.</li>
        </ol>

        <div class="code-block">
            # PowerShell: Force GPO update on all domain computers
            Get-ADComputer -Filter * | ForEach-Object {
            Invoke-Command -ComputerName $_.Name -ScriptBlock { gpupdate /force }
            }

            # This single command can trigger ransomware on every machine in minutes
        </div>

        <div class="technique-card">
            <h4><i class="fas fa-file-export"></i> Double Extortion Model</h4>
            <p style="color: var(--text-secondary); margin: 0;">Before encrypting anything, Gentlemen exfiltrates
                your sensitive data to their infrastructure. This means even if you have perfect backups and can
                restore without paying a dime, they still have leverage.</p>
            <p style="color: var(--text-secondary); margin: 1rem 0 0 0;">"Pay us, or we publish your customer data,
                intellectual property, financial records, and employee information." It's a business model that
                works, unfortunately. And with regulatory fines for data breaches often exceeding ransom demands,
                many organizations calculate that paying is the cheaper option.</p>
        </div>

        <h3>Exfiltration Techniques</h3>
        <p>Gentlemen's data exfiltration is designed to evade detection:</p>
        <ul>
            <li><strong>Cloud Storage Abuse:</strong> Uploading to legitimate services like Mega, pCloud, or even
                Azure Blob storage to blend with normal traffic</li>
            <li><strong>Slow and Steady:</strong> Throttling transfer speeds to avoid triggering DLP alerts or
                bandwidth anomalies</li>
            <li><strong>Compression and Encryption:</strong> Data is compressed and encrypted before transfer,
                making content inspection impossible</li>
            <li><strong>Off-Hours Timing:</strong> Exfiltration often occurs during nights and weekends when
                monitoring is reduced</li>
        </ul>

        <h2>Why Gentlemen Concerns Me More Than Most</h2>

        <p>I've analyzed dozens of ransomware variants over the years. Most follow predictable patterns and
            exploitable weaknesses. But Gentlemen concerns me for several specific reasons:</p>

        <h3>1. The BYOVD Problem Is Getting Worse, Not Better</h3>
        <p>The security industry has known about vulnerable drivers for years. Microsoft maintains a driver
            blocklist. HVCI (Hypervisor-Protected Code Integrity) can prevent many BYOVD attacks. But here's the
            uncomfortable truth: most organizations haven't implemented these controls.</p>

        <p>In my experience consulting with enterprises, I'd estimate fewer than 20% have HVCI enabled, and even
            fewer maintain updated driver blocklists. The gap between what's possible and what's deployed is vast—
            and Gentlemen is exploiting that gap ruthlessly.</p>

        <h3>2. They're Targeting Diverse Industries</h3>
        <p>Unlike ransomware groups that focus on healthcare (for urgency) or law firms (for confidentiality),
            Gentlemen appears to be <strong>opportunistic</strong>. The 17-country spread suggests they're hitting
            whoever they can compromise, whenever they can compromise them.</p>

        <p>Reported victim industries include:</p>
        <ul>
            <li>Manufacturing and industrial</li>
            <li>Professional services (accounting, legal)</li>
            <li>Technology and software</li>
            <li>Healthcare (predictably)</li>
            <li>Financial services</li>
            <li>Education and research</li>
        </ul>

        <p>If you're connected to the internet and have data worth stealing, you're in scope.</p>

        <h3>3. The Go Language Choice Is Strategic</h3>
        <p>Writing ransomware in Go (Golang) provides several operational advantages that make Gentlemen harder to
            detect:</p>

        <ul>
            <li><strong>Cross-Platform Compilation:</strong> A single codebase can target Windows, Linux, and macOS
                with minimal changes</li>
            <li><strong>Static Compilation:</strong> Go binaries are self-contained, reducing dependencies and
                making deployment simpler</li>
            <li><strong>Detection Evasion:</strong> Many security tools have less mature detection signatures for
                Go binaries compared to traditional C/C++ malware</li>
            <li><strong>Reverse Engineering Difficulty:</strong> Go binaries are notoriously difficult to reverse
                engineer, slowing down security research</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>4. Professional Operations Indicate Resources</h3>
        <p>The sophistication of Gentlemen's operations suggests this isn't a few hackers in a basement. They have:
        </p>
        <ul>
            <li>Dedicated infrastructure for command and control</li>
            <li>A leak site for publishing victim data</li>
            <li>What appears to be a negotiation team (based on victim reports)</li>
            <li>Ongoing development of their payload (version updates observed)</li>
        </ul>
        <p>This level of organization typically indicates either a well-funded criminal enterprise or potential
            nation-state backing. Neither scenario is comforting.</p>

        <div class="purple-box">
            <h3 style="color: var(--accent-blue); margin-top: 0;">Timeline: The Gentlemen Campaign</h3>
            <div class="timeline">
                <div class="timeline-item">
                    <div class="date">August 2025</div>
                    <p style="color: var(--text-secondary); margin: 0.5rem 0 0 0;">First samples of Gentlemen
                        ransomware identified in the wild. Initial victims in Western Europe.</p>
                </div>
                <div class="timeline-item">
                    <div class="date">September 2025</div>
                    <p style="color: var(--text-secondary); margin: 0.5rem 0 0 0;">BYOVD techniques confirmed by
                        multiple security researchers. First public leak of victim data.</p>
                </div>
                <div class="timeline-item">
                    <div class="date">October 2025</div>
                    <p style="color: var(--text-secondary); margin: 0.5rem 0 0 0;">Expansion to North America and
                        Asia. GPO manipulation technique documented.</p>
                </div>
                <div class="timeline-item">
                    <div class="date">November 2025</div>
                    <p style="color: var(--text-secondary); margin: 0.5rem 0 0 0;">Victim count reaches double
                        digits. Ransom demands reportedly range from $500K to $5M.</p>
                </div>
                <div class="timeline-item">
                    <div class="date">December 2025</div>
                    <p style="color: var(--text-secondary); margin: 0.5rem 0 0 0;">17 countries confirmed affected.
                        Security vendors release detection updates and IOCs.</p>
                </div>
            </div>
        </div>

        <h2>Defending Against Gentlemen: A Practical Playbook</h2>

        <p>Enough doom and gloom—let's talk about what you can actually do. Here's my practical guidance based on
            Gentlemen's known TTPs, organized by implementation priority:</p>

        <div class="checklist">
            <h3>Immediate Actions (This Week)</h3>
            <ul>
                <li><strong>Enable HVCI:</strong> Hypervisor-Protected Code Integrity prevents most BYOVD attacks by
                    validating driver integrity at the hypervisor level</li>
                <li><strong>Deploy Microsoft's Vulnerable Driver Blocklist:</strong> Via WDAC or Group Policy</li>
                <li><strong>Audit GPO Permissions:</strong> Who can create or modify Group Policy Objects? This list
                    should be extremely small</li>
                <li><strong>Enable EDR Tamper Protection:</strong> Most modern EDR solutions have this—verify it's
                    actually enabled</li>
                <li><strong>Review Domain Admin Usage:</strong> Domain Admin credentials should never be used on
                    regular workstations</li>
            </ul>

            <h3>Short-Term Actions (This Month)</h3>
            <ul>
                <li><strong>Implement Driver Allowlisting:</strong> Only permit known-good drivers to load</li>
                <li><strong>Deploy GPO Change Monitoring:</strong> Alert on any Group Policy modifications</li>
                <li><strong>Segment Privileged Access:</strong> Use PAWs (Privileged Access Workstations) for admin
                    tasks</li>
                <li><strong>Review Backup Isolation:</strong> Can ransomware reach your backups? If yes, fix it</li>
                <li><strong>Test Restoration Procedures:</strong> Backups are worthless if you can't restore from
                    them</li>
            </ul>

            <h3>Long-Term Hardening (This Quarter)</h3>
            <ul>
                <li><strong>Implement Windows Credential Guard:</strong> Protects against credential theft</li>
                <li><strong>Deploy Application Control:</strong> WDAC or AppLocker to prevent unauthorized
                    executables</li>
                <li><strong>Establish Threat Hunting Program:</strong> Proactively look for BYOVD and lateral
                    movement indicators</li>
                <li><strong>Conduct Purple Team Exercises:</strong> Test your detection of BYOVD and GPO abuse</li>
            </ul>
        </div>

        <h3>Detection Opportunities</h3>
        <p>While Gentlemen is sophisticated, they're not invisible. Here's what to monitor for:</p>

        <h4>Driver Loading Events</h4>
        <ul>
            <li>Monitor Windows Event ID 7045 (New Service Installation) for driver installations</li>
            <li>Alert on drivers loaded from unusual paths (%TEMP%, user directories)</li>
            <li>Maintain a baseline of expected drivers and alert on anomalies</li>
        </ul>

        <div class="code-block">
            # Splunk Query: Detect Suspicious Driver Loading
            index=windows EventCode=7045 ServiceType="kernel mode driver"
            | where NOT match(ServiceFile, "(?i)system32\\drivers")
            | stats count by Computer, ServiceName, ServiceFile
        </div>

        <h4>GPO Modification Monitoring</h4>
        <ul>
            <li>Monitor Event IDs 5136/5137 for Active Directory object modifications</li>
            <li>Alert on GPO changes outside approved change windows</li>
            <li>Track changes to SYSVOL (where GPO files are stored)</li>
        </ul>

        <div class="code-block">
            # Splunk Query: Detect GPO Modifications
            index=windows EventCode IN (5136, 5137)
            | where ObjectClass="groupPolicyContainer"
            | stats count by SubjectUserName, ObjectDN, OperationType
            | where NOT SubjectUserName IN ("approved_admin_list")
        </div>

        <h4>EDR Health Monitoring</h4>
        <ul>
            <li>Alert when endpoints stop reporting to your EDR console</li>
            <li>Monitor for EDR service termination events</li>
            <li>Track process termination of known security tool processes</li>
        </ul>

        <h4>Data Exfiltration Indicators</h4>
        <ul>
            <li>Unusual outbound data volumes, especially to cloud storage</li>
            <li>Large file uploads during off-hours</li>
            <li>Connections to known file-sharing services from servers that shouldn't use them</li>
        </ul>

        <div class="info-box">
            <h3 style="color: var(--accent-cyan); margin-top: 0;"><i class="fas fa-shield-alt"></i> EDR
                Considerations</h3>
            <p>If you're evaluating or reconsidering your EDR solution, this is exactly the type of threat that
                separates good platforms from great ones. The ability to:</p>
            <ul style="margin-bottom: 0;">
                <li>Detect and prevent BYOVD attacks before driver loading</li>
                <li>Resist kernel-level tampering attempts</li>
                <li>Maintain visibility even when under attack</li>
                <li>Provide actionable alerts with context</li>
            </ul>
            <p style="margin-bottom: 0; margin-top: 1rem;">Check out our <a
                    href="/comparisons/crowdstrike-vs-microsoft-defender-vs-cortex-xdr.html"
                    style="color: var(--accent-cyan);">EDR/XDR Comparison</a> for an in-depth look at how major
                platforms stack up against BYOVD and other advanced techniques.</p>
        </div>

        <h2>Incident Response: If You're Already Compromised</h2>

        <p>If you suspect a Gentlemen compromise (or any ransomware with similar TTPs), here's the critical first
            response:</p>

        <h3>Immediate Containment</h3>
        <ol>
            <li><strong>Isolate Affected Systems:</strong> Network isolation, not shutdown (preserve memory
                evidence)</li>
            <li><strong>Disable Compromised Accounts:</strong> Especially any Domain Admin accounts that may be
                compromised</li>
            <li><strong>Block Attacker C2:</strong> If you have indicators, block them at the perimeter</li>
            <li><strong>Protect Domain Controllers:</strong> If not yet affected, isolate them immediately</li>
            <li><strong>Preserve Evidence:</strong> Memory dumps and disk images before any remediation</li>
        </ol>

        <h3>Investigation Focus Areas</h3>
        <ul>
            <li>How did initial access occur? (VPN? Phishing? Exposed service?)</li>
            <li>What accounts are compromised? (Check for new accounts, password resets)</li>
            <li>What GPOs were modified? (Compare current state to known-good baseline)</li>
            <li>What data was exfiltrated? (Check network logs, cloud service logs)</li>
            <li>Are backups intact? (Verify before relying on them)</li>
        </ul>

        <p>For detailed response procedures, see our <a href="/guides/ransomware-response-playbook.html"
                style="color: var(--accent-cyan);">Ransomware Response Playbook</a>.</p>

        <h2>The Bigger Picture: Why Ransomware Keeps Winning</h2>

        <p>Every time I write about a new ransomware variant, I'm reminded of a fundamental truth: <strong>we're
                losing this battle</strong>. Not because we lack the tools or the knowledge, but because we lack the
            consistency in applying them.</p>

        <p>Think about it:</p>
        <ul>
            <li>HVCI has existed since Windows 10—most organizations haven't enabled it</li>
            <li>Driver blocklists are free—most organizations don't deploy them</li>
            <li>GPO monitoring is built into Windows—most organizations don't alert on it</li>
            <li>Immutable backups are available—most organizations don't use them</li>
            <li>We know credential theft enables lateral movement—Domain Admins still log into workstations</li>
        </ul>

        <p>The Gentlemen gang isn't using zero-days or nation-state level capabilities. They're using
            <strong>known techniques against known gaps</strong>. And they're succeeding because those gaps persist
            year after year.
        </p>

        <p>The uncomfortable question every security leader should ask: "If Gentlemen targeted us tomorrow, would
            we detect them? Would we stop them? Or would we be calling our incident response retainer and cyber
            insurance carrier?"</p>

        <h2>What I'm Watching Next</h2>

        <p>A few things I'm monitoring as this threat evolves:</p>

        <ul>
            <li><strong>Vulnerable Driver Discovery:</strong> Security researchers continuously find new vulnerable
                drivers. Expect BYOVD attacks to incorporate newer drivers as they're discovered. Microsoft's
                blocklist will always be playing catch-up.</li>
            <li><strong>Affiliate Model Expansion:</strong> Many ransomware operations run affiliate programs,
                recruiting other criminals to deploy their ransomware in exchange for a cut. If Gentlemen adopts
                this model, attack volume could increase dramatically.</li>
            <li><strong>Linux/ESXi Variants:</strong> <span style="color: var(--accent-cyan);">CONFIRMED December
                    2025:</span> The group has now released enhanced support for Linux and ESXi environments,
                allowing them to target VMware infrastructure directly. Organizations with mixed environments are
                now at increased risk.</li>
            <li><strong>Encryption Speed Improvements:</strong> <span style="color: var(--accent-cyan);">December
                    2025:</span> Security researchers report a 9-15% encryption speed increase across variants, with
                dual execution modes for local and network-wide encryption.</li>
            <li><strong>Targeting Patterns:</strong> As more victim data emerges, we'll understand whether certain
                industries or regions are being specifically targeted or if this remains opportunistic.</li>
        </ul>

        <div class="info-box">
            <h3 style="color: var(--accent-cyan); margin-top: 0;"><i class="fas fa-sync-alt"></i> December 18, 2025
                Update</h3>
            <p><strong>New developments confirmed by security researchers:</strong></p>
            <ul style="margin-bottom: 0;">
                <li><strong>Linux/ESXi Support:</strong> Enhanced cross-platform capabilities now include direct
                    VMware ESXi targeting</li>
                <li><strong>Encryption Speed:</strong> 9-15% performance improvement across all variants</li>
                <li><strong>Dual Execution:</strong> New modes for local-only or network-wide encryption</li>
                <li><strong>Anti-AV Tools:</strong> Custom tools using signed driver abuse and registry
                    modifications</li>
                <li><strong>Detection Signature:</strong> AhnLab identifies as Ransomware/Win.GentlemenCrypt (V3
                    engine Dec 2025)</li>
            </ul>
        </div>

        <h2>Final Thoughts</h2>

        <p>The Gentlemen ransomware gang represents the continuing evolution of ransomware threats. They're
            technically capable, operationally sophisticated, and clearly well-resourced. The combination of BYOVD,
            GPO manipulation, and double extortion makes them a formidable adversary.</p>

        <p>But here's what I keep coming back to—<strong>everything they're doing is preventable</strong>. Every
            technique they use has corresponding defenses. The BYOVD attacks fail against HVCI-enabled systems. The
            GPO abuse fails if privileged access is properly controlled. The exfiltration fails if proper DLP and
            network segmentation are in place.</p>

        <p>The question isn't whether we know how to defend against these attacks. The question is whether we have
            the organizational will to implement those defenses before we become victims.</p>

        <p>I'll continue tracking this group and will update this article as we learn more. In the meantime, take
            a hard look at your driver policies, your AD security, and your data loss prevention capabilities. The
            Gentlemen are actively hunting, and despite their ironic name, they're not going to be polite about it.
        </p>

        <div class="alert-box">
            <p><strong>Stay vigilant. Stay prepared. And whatever you do, don't assume it won't happen to
                    you.</strong></p>
            <p style="margin-top: 1rem; margin-bottom: 0;"><em>Have you seen indicators of Gentlemen ransomware in
                    your environment? Dealing with a BYOVD attack? The security community benefits when we share
                    intelligence—responsibly, of course. The more we understand about how these attacks unfold in
                    the real world, the better we can defend against them.</em></p>
        </div>
    </div>
